extracted.intended_audience: general readers, comedians, and researchers interested in comedy ethics and plagiarism
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and evaluating instances where a comedian or media performer uses another's comic material without acknowledgement or consent, and understanding defenses, historical norms, and consequences. Covers stand-up, television/film, and other media contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of joke theft
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke theft is the act of performing and taking credit for comic material written or performed by another person without their consent and without acknowledging the other person's authorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be a form of plagiarism and, in some cases, copyright infringement. Use this definition as the baseline test: (1) material originated with another person, (2) performed/claimed without consent, (3) no acknowledgement. Examples in the article cite stand-up routines and media bits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling as a 'hack' (social sanction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic who is known to steal jokes may be labelled with the epithet 'hack' by other comics. A 'hack comic' uses material that is unoriginal or which is blatantly copied from its original author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an industry/community judgment rather than a legal finding; social ostracism and damage to reputation are common consequences cited in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity from simultaneous/coincidental discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Some cases of alleged joke theft are ambiguous, due to the possibility of simultaneous and coincidental discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article and a 2018 study note that similarity alone may not prove theft; consider independent creation and the prevalence of certain joke tropes. Accusations can reflect peers' perceptions of a comic's community membership and craft as much as textual similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses: satire, calque, borrowing, inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Some comics have defended their re-use of other people's jokes as satire or as a calque (word-for-word translation). Others have claimed their re-use was a type of 'borrowing,' or taking inspiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a disputed bit, consider whether the alleged reuse is transformation (satire/parody), translation, or merely close copying; documented intent and degree of transformation matter in community and sometimes legal contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical (vaudeville) etiquette: 'add to the joke and make it his own'
rubrics_metrics.description: In music halls and vaudeville it was common for performers to 'borrow' material; etiquette only required that 'the borrower add to the joke and make it his own.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical norms allowed more fluid reuse; when assessing older practices or stylistic borrowing, weigh era-specific conventions. Lack of proof of origin was common (one-liners, scant documentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: First-to-media association increases theft impact
rubrics_metrics.description: A new type of joke theft arose when the first comic to tell a stolen joke on media became the one associated with the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When media exposure gives public association, consider timing of broadcasts/releases and who first reached mass media. This raises stakes even if origin is contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized recordings facilitate modern joke theft
rubrics_metrics.description: The widespread use of video camera-equipped smartphones led to an increase in unauthorized recordings of live comedy shows, some of which were shared online, which may have facilitated joke theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical mitigation: comedians may request no unauthorized audio/video recordings to reduce risk. When evaluating alleged theft, look for online provenance and dates of recordings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited legal recourse historically
rubrics_metrics.description: There is, historically, very little legal recourse taken in cases of joke theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While copyright or other legal claims are possible in some cases, the article emphasizes rarity of successful legal enforcement; often disputes are settled socially, financially, or informally (e.g., sued and sometimes compensated, but many cases remain unlitigated).

rubrics_metrics.name: Community enforcement and extrajudicial consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Some comics have chosen to exact their own justice (threats, physical altercations, bans), and community reactions (bans, reputational damage) are common forms of recourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: confrontations, bans from clubs (Joe Rogan banned from The Comedy Store after confronting Carlos Mencia), alleged physical retaliation. Assess likely community sanctions when formal legal paths are unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution difficulties and false attribution by media
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists and other media sometimes falsely attribute jokes to the wrong comics, complicating origin claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When investigating origin, verify primary performance evidence; be wary of secondary reporting that may misattribute material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of overlap: 'finite number of jokes' / inevitability of similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses sometimes assert that there are only 'a finite number of jokes' making overlap inevitable; directors/producers have invoked homage or use of source material as guide tracks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether similarity reflects common tropes or direct copying. Consider degree of uniqueness, phrasing, structure, and whether reuse rises to verbatim appropriation versus trope-level overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theft beyond jokes: persona/attitude appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations may extend beyond individual jokes to stealing a performer's persona or act (e.g., claims Denis Leary stole Bill Hicks's persona and attitude).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess broader patterns (style, themes, stage persona) not just discrete jokes; persona-theft can damage careers and provoke stronger peer backlash even where individual jokes are ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke theft across media (film, TV, print) and cross-genre appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Joke theft is not limited to stand-up; jokes in film and television shows are often taken from comics or other media, and shows have been accused of lifting gags or premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a case in film/TV, look for prior performances, published material, and timing. Consider whether the use is an homage, adaptation, or verbatim lift (examples: Naked Gun/Get Smart parallels; Simpsons/Family Guy disputes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of documented evidence (recordings, albums, publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of origin is often scarce for older one-liners and live material; recorded albums, broadcasts, or publications can provide evidence linking material to an originator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to contemporaneous recordings, release dates on albums, and documented performances. The article cites cases where albums or broadcasts were central to disputes (e.g., Bill Cosby/George Carlin, Louis C.K./Dane Cook).
